individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper proposes MoWM, a hybrid world-model framework for embodied action planning. It combines a pixel-space video diffusion world model (SVD, following VPP) with a latent-space world model built on V-JEPA2 and a transformer predictor. The latent model is trained to predict future states in compressed space; during action planning, pixel features from the diffusion U-Net and latent features are aligned, concatenated, projected, and combined via a residual/gating mechanism, then fed into a Diffusion Policy action decoder. The framework is trained in two stages on CALVIN, and experiments on ABC→D generalization show improved task success rates over prior imitation, VLA, and world-model baselines. Ablations compare concat fusion, cross-attention fusion, and no fusion, showing concat works best.
Strengths: Addresses a relevant and well-motivated problem: visual redundancy in pixel-based video world models for action planning, and proposes a concrete two-stage pipeline that combines complementary representations (motion-aware latent and fine-grained pixel).

The empirical evaluation on CALVIN includes a broad set of baselines across imitation, VLA, and world-model categories, and reports both task success rates and average completion length; MoWM shows consistent gains, especially on the 5th sub-task and longer horizons.

The ablation study on fusion mechanisms (concat vs cross-attention vs no fusion) provides useful evidence that the latent-space features contribute beyond the pixel-space model, and the qualitative analysis of static-frame failures in the pixel model motivates the design.
The framework reuses established components (SVD, V-JEPA2, Diffusion Policy), making the approach relatively easy to build upon if details are provided.
Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single simulation benchmark (CALVIN ABC→D); no real-robot experiments, additional benchmarks, or cross-embodiment results. Claims of superior generalization are therefore not fully supported.

The technical presentation is incomplete and at times confusing: equations use the same symbol t for video time and action denoising step; the alignment of latent tokens (N_s = h×w) with pixel feature maps is not explained; the exact temporal handling, sequence length T, and how the latent world model generates T future states are unresolved.

The novelty is incremental: the 'mixture' is a late fusion of existing feature extractors with linear projections/concat/residual/gating; several design choices (e.g., why concat beats cross-attention) are not analyzed deeply, and no comparison to other hybrid feature fusion approaches is provided.

The main results may be confounded by differences in model capacity, pretraining data, and compute; no information is given about baseline fine-tuning details, model sizes, training resources, or number of seeds, and no error bars/statistical tests are reported.

Some claims are overstated: 'state-of-the-art' is claimed based on one dataset; the average length metric is not defined; the contribution of the latent world model's predictive training versus its pretrained encoder (V-JEPA2) is not ablated (e.g., using V-JEPA2 features directly without the latent transformer).
Questions: How are the pixel and latent feature sequences aligned along the temporal dimension? Does the latent world model output T consecutive future states in one forward pass (teacher-forced) or via autoregressive rollouts, and how is this matched to the T frames of the pixel model?

What is the exact architecture of the action decoder and how are raw actions represented (action horizon, normalization, receding horizon control)? Is the diffusion policy conditioned only on φ_final, and how is the gating matrix initialized?

Were all baseline results reproduced under the same training setup, or were numbers taken from original papers? If reproduced, what compute was used per baseline? If not, how can we rule out implementation mismatches?

Why does concatenation outperform cross-attention? Is this because of optimization difficulty, and could a better-designed attention mechanism close the gap? Have you tested learned per-channel weighting or FiLM-style modulation?

Does the performance gain come from the latent world model's training on CALVIN, or simply from using V-JEPA2 features? Please run an ablation where the latent branch is a frozen V-JEPA2 encoder without the transformer predictor, and another where the latent branch does not use pretrained weights.
What is the inference-time computational overhead of running both world models compared to VPP alone? Is MoWM practical for closed-loop control?
How many random seeds were used for MoWM and ablations? Are the reported differences statistically significant?
Limitations: Only evaluated in simulation on CALVIN; real-world deployment and other embodiments are untested, so the generalization claims are limited.

The method requires running both a large video diffusion model (SVD) and a 400M-parameter latent transformer, which may be computationally expensive for real-time control; inference cost is not analyzed.

The latent decoder used for visualization is separately trained and not validated; the quality of latent predictions is not quantified with standard metrics, so the qualitative comparison in Figure 3 is anecdotal.
The fusion approach is fixed after training; it may not adapt to unseen dynamics or task variations, and no mechanism for dynamic weighting based on task complexity is provided.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts, though the application is in robotic manipulation (standard dual-use considerations).

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper proposes MoWM, a hybrid world model framework for embodied action planning. It combines a pixel-space video diffusion world model (based on Stable Video Diffusion) and a latent-space world model (based on V-JEPA2) to fuse motion-aware high-level features with fine-grained low-level visual features. The fused representation conditions a diffusion policy for action decoding. Experiments on the CALVIN benchmark show state-of-the-art task success rates and generalization to unseen scenes, with ablations demonstrating the benefit of the fusion approach.
Strengths: Clear and well-motivated combination of complementary pixel-space and latent-space world models, addressing visual redundancy in pixel-level reconstruction.
Comprehensive evaluation on CALVIN with a wide range of baselines spanning imitation learning, VLA, and world-model-based methods, showing consistent improvements.
Ablation studies compare different fusion strategies (concat, cross-attention, no fusion) and confirm the effectiveness of the hybrid approach.
Qualitative analysis highlights the motion-aware advantage of the latent world model over the pixel world model, supporting the design rationale.
The paper is generally well-written and provides sufficient implementation details for reproducibility.
Weaknesses: The fusion method is a simple concatenation followed by a linear projection, which is not particularly novel; the 'mixture-of-world-model' term may be overstated compared to the actual complexity.
Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (CALVIN ABC->D) in simulation; no real-robot experiments or additional benchmarks are provided, limiting the demonstrated generalizability.
The paper does not include an ablation using only latent features, making it unclear how much of the performance gain comes from the latent model alone versus the fusion.

The 'without fusion' ablation (0.560 on 5th task) appears stronger than the VPP baseline in Table 1 (0.518), suggesting potential inconsistencies in training setup or hyperparameters that are not fully discussed.
Some notation confusion: Equation (7) reuses epsilon_theta, which was previously used for the pixel world model denoiser, and the action denoiser is not clearly differentiated.
The computational cost of running both world models during inference is not discussed, which could be a practical limitation.
Questions: How does the performance of MoWM compare to using only latent features for action decoding? What is the marginal contribution of the pixel features beyond the latent features?
Why does concatenation-based fusion outperform cross-attention? Could the cross-attention variant be improved with different initialization or more training steps?
What is the inference-time computational cost (FLOPs, latency) of the full MoWM system compared to VPP or other baselines?
How sensitive are the results to the choice of latent world model (e.g., V-JEPA2 vs a lighter alternative)?
Is the static-frame issue in the pixel world model a frequent failure mode? Can the paper provide a quantitative analysis of how often this occurs?
Limitations: The method is evaluated only on simulated CALVIN tasks; real-world applicability is not demonstrated.
The use of large pre-trained models (SVD, V-JEPA2) imposes significant computational and memory requirements, which may hinder practical deployment.
The paper does not analyze failure cases or provide uncertainty estimates for action predictions.
The fusion scheme is fixed; an adaptive weighting based on task complexity would be more flexible and potentially more effective.
The latent world model is trained on the same CALVIN data, so the benefit may partly derive from overfitting to the benchmark's specific dynamics.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes MoWM, a hybrid world-model framework for embodied action planning. It combines a pixel-space video diffusion world model (based on SVD) and a latent-space world model (based on V-JEPA2) to predict future states, then fuses their features and decodes actions with a Diffusion Policy. The two world models are trained separately on CALVIN, frozen, and then their features are concatenated, linearly projected, and combined with a residual connection before an action denoising module. Experiments on the CALVIN ABC→D split report state-of-the-art success rates, and ablations compare concat-based fusion, cross-attention fusion, and no fusion.
Strengths: The motivation is clear and relevant: pixel world models can be distracted by visual redundancy while latent world models may lose fine-grained details, so combining complementary representations is a reasonable direction.

The proposed method achieves strong empirical results on CALVIN, outperforming the strongest baselines (e.g., Pi0 and VPP) by 5.7% and 13.4% average task success rate, with the largest gain on the 5th sub-task.
The paper includes a broad set of baselines covering imitation learning, VLA, and world-model methods, and an ablation of fusion designs (concat vs. cross-attention vs. no fusion).
Qualitative analysis of pixel and latent future-state predictions provides some insight into why latent motion-awareness helps, e.g., the pixel world model sometimes generates static frames.
The code is promised to be released, which aids reproducibility.
Weaknesses: The novelty is limited: the final fusion in Eq. (5)-(6) is essentially concatenation plus a linear projection and a residual addition. The paper repeatedly claims that latent features 'modulate' or 'guide the extraction' of pixel features, but no actual modulation or guidance of the pixel-space feature extraction is implemented.

Several technical details are ambiguous or missing: how the latent world model produces features for T future steps in a single forward pass (autoregressive or not), how latent tokens are spatially aligned to the pixel feature grid for concatenation, whether the V-JEPA2 encoder is frozen or fine-tuned, and what the 'gating matrix' W_gate in Eq. (6) exactly is and how it is initialized.

The ablation is incomplete. There is no baseline using only the latent world model features with the same action decoder, so the paper cannot demonstrate that both feature streams are necessary; it only shows that adding latent features to pixel features helps.

Evaluation is limited to the CALVIN benchmark; no real-robot experiments, additional simulation benchmarks, or zero-shot transfer results are reported. All numbers lack error bars or statistical significance tests, making it unclear whether the improvements are robust.

The comparison to latent world-model-based planners is missing (e.g., DINO-WM or similar), despite being cited in related work, so the claim that fusing latent and pixel features is superior to using latent features alone is not directly tested.
The paper does not report the computational cost of the full MoWM system (parameters, inference time, memory) relative to baselines, which is important since it runs two large world models.

The qualitative evidence in Figure 4 appears cherry-picked and is not systematically quantified; additionally, it refers to generated videos, while the action decoder uses single-step denoising features, leaving a disconnect.
Questions: How exactly is the latent world model used to generate Φ_latent for T future steps? Is it run autoregressively, and what is the conditioning context length k?
Is the V-JEPA2 encoder frozen during latent world model training and during stage 2? Are gradients ever propagated into the encoder?
How are latent token features arranged into the N_s = h × w spatial dimension? Are the latent tokens reshaped to match the pixel feature grid, and if so, how are the spatial resolutions reconciled?
What is the mathematical role of W_gate in Eq. (6)? Is it a per-feature gate, a scalar, or simply a learned matrix? Is it initialized to zero to make the residual start as identity?
Why is there no ablation using only the latent world model features with the same action decoder? This is needed to justify the claim that pixel features are still necessary.
How many random seeds are the success rates averaged over, and what are the standard deviations or confidence intervals?
How does MoWM compare to DINO-WM or other latent-world-model-only action planners on CALVIN?
What is the total parameter count and inference latency of MoWM compared with VPP and Pi0?
Does the method transfer to other benchmarks or real-robot platforms? If not, what are the main obstacles?
Limitations: Only evaluated on the CALVIN benchmark (simulated, single robot embodiment); generalization to other simulators or real robots is untested.
The fusion is a static learned projection/concatenation; there is no adaptive or task-dependent weighting between latent and pixel features.
The two world models are trained separately, which may be suboptimal compared to jointly training or coadapting them.
The paper does not analyze the additional computational overhead of running two world models, including training time, memory footprint, and inference cost.
The latent space is not directly interpretable; a decoder was trained only for visualization and is not used during planning, so the qualitative figures may not reflect what the action decoder sees.
No negative societal impacts or safety considerations for real-world robotic deployment are discussed.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper proposes MoWM, a hybrid world model framework for embodied action planning. It combines a pixel-space diffusion world model (SVD) with a latent-space world model based on V-JEPA 2. The two models are pre-trained separately for instruction-conditioned future prediction; then their features are aligned and fused via concatenation and a residual connection, and a Diffusion Policy decoder is trained end-to-end. Experiments on the CALVIN benchmark show state-of-the-art task success rates, and ablations indicate that fusing latent features improves performance over using pixel features alone.
Strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem of visual redundancy in pixel-space world models and proposes a hybrid framework combining pixel and latent world models to improve action planning.
The proposed MoWM achieves state-of-the-art task success rates on the CALVIN benchmark, with particularly strong gains in long-horizon tasks.
The ablation study and qualitative visualization provide insight into the complementary strengths of pixel and latent features.
The paper compares against a broad set of baselines across imitation learning, VLA, and world model paradigms.
Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single simulation benchmark (CALVIN ABC->D); no real-robot experiments or other environments are provided.
No error bars or multiple-seed results are reported, making it impossible to assess statistical significance of the improvements.
The fusion scheme is a simple concatenation plus residual connection; the claim of 'mixture-of-world-model' is overstated and lacks architectural novelty or adaptive weighting.

The mechanism by which latent features 'guide extraction' of pixel features is vague; the paper only concatenates features after both models are frozen, rather than truly modulating the pixel model's internal representation.
Important implementation details are missing: how baselines were adapted/fine-tuned, exact feature dimensions, the value of T, and the initialization of the gating matrix.
The paper does not include a latent-only baseline for action decoding, so the complementarity of the two feature spaces is not directly demonstrated.
Potential issue with notation: time step t is used both for diffusion noise level and future frame index, causing confusion.
Questions: How were baselines adapted or fine-tuned for the CALVIN ABC->D split? Were official checkpoints used or were models retrained, and what hyperparameters were used for fair comparison?
What is the exact architecture of the linear projections and gating mechanism? Is W_gate a matrix or a scalar, and how is it initialized?
What is the value of T (number of future frames) used in experiments, and how does it affect computational cost and performance?
Why does concatenation-based fusion outperform cross-attention fusion? Is the difference statistically significant given the absence of error bars?
Are the world models kept completely frozen during the second stage, or do gradients flow into them? If frozen, how does the fusion module align the two feature spaces?
How does MoWM perform on simpler single-task benchmarks or in settings with out-of-distribution instructions?
What is the inference-time overhead compared to VPP, given that two world models are run?
The latent world model uses V-JEPA 2 features; what is the token sequence length N_s for 200x200 images, and how is text conditioning incorporated into the latent model?
Limitations: Only evaluated on CALVIN, a single simulated benchmark; no real-world validation or other simulation environments.
No statistical significance testing (e.g., multiple seeds, confidence intervals) is reported.
The 'mixture' aspect is a simple feature concatenation, not an adaptive or learned gating mechanism that truly selects between models.
The paper does not study how performance degrades when the latent or pixel model is removed entirely, only the fusion variant.
The computational cost of running two large world models is not analyzed in terms of inference efficiency.
Failure cases and limitations in complex or cluttered scenes are not discussed.

review.Summary: The paper proposes MoWM, a framework that combines pixel-space and latent-space world models for embodied action planning. It first trains a pixel-space video diffusion world model (based on SVD) and a latent-space world model (based on V-JEPA2 features and a transformer predictor) separately on CALVIN. In a second stage, features from both models are fused via concatenation, projected, and combined with a residual connection to pixel features; a diffusion policy then decodes actions from these fused representations. Experiments on the CALVIN benchmark ABC→D split report state-of-the-art success rates, especially on long-horizon tasks, along with ablations of fusion strategies.
Strengths: The motivation is clear and relevant: pixel-space world models may introduce task-irrelevant visual redundancy, while latent world models may lose fine-grained details; combining them is a sensible direction.
The paper includes a useful ablation of fusion designs (concat, cross-attention, no fusion), showing concatenation works best, and provides some training details (GPU counts, batch size, optimizer).
The method outperforms strong baselines including Pi0, VPP, and OpenVLA on CALVIN, with larger gains on the 5th sub-task, suggesting benefits for long-horizon planning.
The qualitative analysis comparing latent and pixel future-state predictions offers intuitive support for the motion-aware advantage of the latent model.
Weaknesses: The novelty is limited: the 'mixture-of-world-models' is essentially feature concatenation plus linear projection, not a sophisticated fusion mechanism or a true mixture-of-experts architecture.
Evaluation is confined to the CALVIN simulated benchmark; no real-robot experiments or other sim benchmarks are presented, weakening claims of generalization.

Several implementation details are missing: which text encoder is used, how text is injected into the latent world model, the exact 'single-step denoising' procedure for pixel features, and the evaluation protocol (closed-loop vs open-loop, action chunk length, replanning frequency).
No statistical significance tests, standard deviations, or multiple seeds are reported, so it is unclear if improvements over baselines are robust.
The claim that latent features provide 'motion-aware guidance' is supported only by anecdotal qualitative examples, not by a quantitative metric or controlled experiment.
The ablation 'without fusion' still uses the pixel world model features; a baseline with only latent features is missing, which would better isolate the contribution of each component.
Questions: Which text encoder is used to encode instructions for the pixel and latent world models? Is it pre-trained and frozen or fine-tuned?
How are text tokens injected into the latent world model transformer? Are they prepended to the state token sequence and processed via self-attention, or through cross-attention?
In the second stage, what exactly is the 'single-step denoising process' for the pixel world model? Is it a full denoising step or an intermediate timestep? How is the noise level chosen?
What is the action chunk length T and how often does the policy replan during evaluation? Is the evaluation closed-loop (using predicted future states from the current observation) or open-loop?
Were all baseline results taken from their original papers, or were baselines re-run under the same codebase and compute budget? If re-run, what seeds and evaluation episodes were used?
What is the variance of the reported success rates across multiple runs or seeds? Have significance tests (e.g., paired t-tests) been conducted against the closest baselines?
How does a version using only latent-world-model features perform? This would clarify whether the improvement from fusion is due to adding latent information or simply to having more parameters.

How was the V-JEPA2 encoder used? Is it frozen or fine-tuned during latent world model training? Does the latent predictor condition on instructions via cross-attention or by concatenation with text embeddings?
What is the total compute cost including pixel world model fine-tuning? The paper gives details only for the latent model and second stage training.
Limitations: The method is evaluated only on CALVIN, a simulated grid-world-like benchmark; its applicability to real-world manipulation or more diverse simulated environments is unverified.
The design depends on two large pre-trained models (SVD and V-JEPA2), which are heavy and may not be available or affordable for many robotics labs.
The fusion scheme is fixed and not task-adaptive; the paper only mentions adaptive fusion as future work.
No failure-case analysis is provided, so it is unclear what types of tasks or scenarios cause the method to fail.
Potential negative societal impacts of robotics manipulation research are not discussed, though the risk is low.

review.Summary: The paper proposes MoWM, a hybrid world-model framework for embodied action planning. It combines a pixel-space video diffusion world model (based on SVD) with a latent-space world model (based on V-JEPA2 features and a transformer predictor). The two models are trained separately for instruction-conditioned future prediction, then their features are aligned, concatenated, projected, and combined via a residual connection before a diffusion policy decodes actions. Experiments on the CALVIN benchmark ABC→D split show improved task success rates over prior imitation, VLA, and world-model baselines, with ablations comparing concatenation, cross-attention, and no fusion.
Strengths: Addresses a relevant and well-motivated problem: visual redundancy in pixel-space world models and complementary strengths of latent motion-aware representations.
Reports strong empirical gains on CALVIN over a broad set of baselines spanning imitation learning, VLA, and world-model methods, especially on the long-horizon 5th sub-task.
Includes an ablation of fusion mechanisms (concat vs cross-attention vs no fusion), providing some evidence that latent features contribute beyond pixel features alone.
Qualitative analysis illustrates failure modes of the pixel world model (e.g., static frames) and the motion-awareness of the latent model, supporting the design rationale.
The framework leverages established components (SVD, V-JEPA2, Diffusion Policy), making the approach relatively easy to build upon if implementation details are clarified.
Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single simulated benchmark (CALVIN ABC→D) with no real-robot experiments, additional benchmarks, or cross-embodiment results; claims of superior generalization are not fully supported.
No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported, so the robustness of the improvements over baselines is unclear.
The novelty is incremental: the 'mixture-of-world-models' is essentially feature concatenation plus linear projection and a residual connection, not an adaptive or truly integrated fusion mechanism.
A baseline using only latent-world-model features with the same action decoder is missing, so the complementarity of the two feature streams is not directly demonstrated.

Several technical details are ambiguous or missing: notation conflates diffusion time and future-frame time; temporal alignment and generation of T latent future states are unclear; fusion dimensions and the gating matrix are not fully specified; and baseline adaptation and evaluation protocols are incomplete.
The computational cost of running both large world models during inference is not analyzed, which is important for practical closed-loop control.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, such as 'state-of-the-art' based on a single benchmark and the description of latent features as 'guiding' or 'modulating' pixel feature extraction when the actual mechanism is late concatenation.
Questions: How exactly does the latent world model generate future features for T steps? Is it autoregressive or one-shot, and how is it temporally aligned with the pixel world model's T frames?
Is the V-JEPA2 encoder frozen or fine-tuned during latent-world-model training and during stage 2? How is text conditioning incorporated into the latent model?
Why does concatenation outperform cross-attention? Is the difference statistically significant given no error bars?
What is the performance of a latent-only variant using the same action decoder? This is needed to justify the claim that pixel features are still necessary.
Were baseline results reproduced under the same setup or taken from original papers? If reproduced, what compute, seeds, and evaluation episodes were used?
What is the inference-time computational overhead (parameters, FLOPs, latency) of MoWM compared to VPP and other strong baselines?
How sensitive are the results to the choice of latent world model or to the number of future frames T?
Limitations: Only evaluated in simulation on CALVIN; real-world deployment and other embodiments are untested.
Requires running two large pre-trained models (SVD and V-JEPA2), which imposes significant computational and memory burdens for real-time or resource-constrained robotics applications.
The fusion is fixed after training and not task-adaptive; no mechanism for dynamic weighting based on task complexity or uncertainty is provided.
No failure-case analysis or uncertainty estimates for action predictions are presented.
The latent world model is trained on the same CALVIN data, so performance may partly reflect overfitting to the benchmark's specific dynamics.
Potential negative societal impacts are not discussed, though the application is standard robotic manipulation.
